rows.description: A scary scene makes me hide and I have nightmares. I do not know what is pretend. Wise adults choose age-fit shows, sit with me and say "it is a story, you are safe".

A game pops up a chat or a stranger says "send me a photo" or "don't tell your parents". I may not know it is unsafe. Wise rule: always show a trusted adult. Any request for secrets is a warning sign.
I want to be like my favourite cartoon hero and copy his moves and words. I feel excited and inspired. Wise adults enjoy this and remind me, gently, that cartoon things cannot be done in real life.

I cannot stop watching cartoons and get upset when it ends. The screen holds my attention fast and switching off feels like losing something. Wise parents set clear time and give a warning and a fun next thing.

Someone mocks your faith as foolish. It stings and tempts you to argue or hit back. Answer briefly, without defensiveness, set limits on jokes, and remember that their dismissal says more about them than your worth.

You have drifted from belief and miss the comfort of ritual and community. Grief for that loss is real. Find new sources of meaning, such as service, art, reflection or friends, without pretending the old ones did not matter.

People shun or lecture you for doubt or a different path. It hurts as loss of belonging. Seek members who hold questions kindly, keep some connection, and remember that group acceptance is not the measure of your sincerity.

A friend with no faith or a different faith asks honest questions. Listen without trying to convert or win, share what your belief means to you, and enjoy the differences. Respect grows from curiosity, not debate.

You want to speak but freeze, imagining humiliation. Wise: accept a no would hurt but not define you, and ask simply once. Immature: hinting endlessly or using friends as messengers to avoid all risk.

Long-distance or online crush seems perfect because you see only highlights. Wise: notice the gap between image and person and meet in ordinary settings. Immature: dropping the real person when they show flaws.
Someone says they do not feel the same and it stings. Wise: give a gracious no, without lying about reasons or leaving hope. Harmful: leading them on because you enjoy being wanted.

Thoughts loop on them, you check their profile and mood constantly. Wise: notice it is fantasy feeding on uncertainty, widen your life, talk to a friend. Harmful: tracking their movements or turning up uninvited.

My parent controls my choices with guilt, threats of illness, or silence and I feel guilty for wanting independence. This pattern is not love, and it is not my fault. I set gentle firm boundaries, keep warmth where possible, and seek support.

My parent denies things they said or did and tells me I am too sensitive, and I doubt my own memory. I keep notes, trust my direct experience, talk to a trusted person, and do not need their agreement to believe myself.

My relatives compare my salary, marriage, or looks with others and I feel small. I answer briefly, with humour or firmness, and remember that questions like these say more about their anxieties than about my value.

I begin to see that my parent's harshness came from their own pain and poverty and I feel sad and softer. Understanding is not excusing; I can be kind while still holding boundaries and not repeating the same pattern.
Warm cheer after a success makes the child beam and want to try again. Keep praise simple and unpressured; accidents are ignored kindly because bodies mature on their own timetable.
Scolding or laughing at accidents teaches the child that her body is disgusting and that mistakes must be hidden. Wise caregivers calmly clean up, say it is okay, and try again another day.
The toddler refuses the potty or holds on, claiming control over her own body. Pressure sharpens resistance. Offer choices, keep it low-key, and pause if the child is clearly not ready.
I made a tower all by myself and shout "look at me!" I feel tall and happy. Wise adults look and say what they see, "you worked hard on it". Proud feelings drive me to try more.
I show my badge to a friend and he looks away sadly. I feel confused. A wise child says "you can get one too" and asks about his own work. Sharing pride without bragging keeps friendships warm.
I show my work and my sister says "mine is better". I feel smaller. Wise parents praise each child for their own effort and do not turn pride into a contest.
